sections.b: 1 Kings gives Elijah three chapters of almost unbroken story. He announces the drought by oath before Ahab (1 Kings 17:1), hides at the Kerith Brook, and is fed by ravens and then by a widow of Zarephath in Phoenicia, whose son he raises (1 Kings 17:2–24). In the third year he meets Obadiah and Ahab, gathers Israel to Mount Carmel, mocks the prophets of Baal, rebuilds the LORD's altar with twelve stones and prays down fire; the prophets of Baal are killed and the rain returns (1 Kings 18). Jezebel's threat sends him to Horeb, where God meets him in "a sound of thin silence" (1 Kings 19:12), gives him three people to anoint and tells him seven thousand remain faithful; he then calls Elisha with his cloak (1 Kings 19).

Elijah's last scene in 1 Kings is in Naboth's vineyard, where he confronts Ahab with the question, "Have you murdered, and taken possession as well?" (1 Kings 21:19), and announces the end of Ahab's house and of Jezebel. When Ahab humbles himself, the word of the LORD comes to Elijah again to tell him the disaster is delayed (1 Kings 21:27–29). Elijah is not present in chapter 22, where another lone prophet, Micaiah, faces the king.

common: Elijah means "my God is the LORD," and his name sums up his message (1 Kings 18:39).
The Transfiguration pairs Elijah with Moses as the two great witnesses of the Law and the Prophets.
uncommon: Some readers think God's question at Horeb and Elijah's unchanged answer show that Elijah was being gently retired, not rebuked.
A few interpreters have read the "ravens" of 1 Kings 17:4 as human helpers (Arabs or men of a place called Orev).

claude.title: After Horeb, words instead of fire
claude.body: My reading of Horeb, that the "sound of thin silence" answers Baal's "not a sound" on Carmel, is set out in the note on 1 Kings 19:12. One further point: after Horeb, Elijah never again calls down fire in 1 Kings. His next task is a spoken word to Ahab in a vineyard (1 Kings 21:17–24), and that word, not a spectacle, brings the king to repentance (1 Kings 21:27). That may be what Horeb changed, though 2 Kings 1:10–12 shows fire still in Elijah's hands.

sections.b: Ahab is on stage in every chapter from 17 to 22, but the narrator shows him in many lights. He searches for grass for his horses during the drought and blames Elijah for it (1 Kings 18:5, 18:17). He watches the fire fall on Carmel and drives home in the rain with the prophet running before him (1 Kings 18:45–46). In chapter 20 he is a capable war leader who listens to elders and prophets, then spares Ben-hadad by treaty and is condemned (1 Kings 20:31–43). In chapter 21 he sulks over Naboth's vineyard, lets Jezebel act in his name, and then humbles himself before God (1 Kings 21:4, 21:27–29). In chapter 22 he hates the one prophet who tells him the truth, disguises himself, and dies on his feet in his chariot (1 Kings 22:8, 22:30–37).

The Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III names "Ahab the Israelite" among the kings who fought Assyria at Qarqar in 853 BC, with 2,000 chariots, the largest chariot force in the coalition, and 10,000 soldiers, beside Hadadezer of Damascus. This is the earliest datable mention of an Israelite king outside the Bible. It fits the treaty of 1 Kings 20:34 and the three years of peace in 1 Kings 22:1, but it raises questions about the wars with "Ben-hadad" and about whether Ahab died at Ramoth-gilead, which historians still debate.

common: Ahab is remembered as the worst king of Israel, chiefly because of Jezebel and Baal (1 Kings 16:30; 1 Kings 21:25).
uncommon: Following J. Maxwell Miller, some historians think the battle stories of 1 Kings 20 and 22 first belonged to a later king and were attached to Ahab.

sections.b: Before she was a name in Revelation, Jezebel was a real queen. The daughter of Ethbaal, "king of the Sidonians" (1 Kings 16:31), whom Josephus, quoting the Phoenician historian Menander, calls a priest of Astarte who seized the throne of Tyre, she married Ahab and brought the worship of Baal to Samaria. Kings says she killed the LORD's prophets (1 Kings 18:4, 18:13), fed the prophets of Asherah, and perhaps those of Baal too, at her table (1 Kings 18:19), swore by her gods to kill Elijah (1 Kings 19:2), and arranged the judicial murder of Naboth with letters under Ahab's seal (1 Kings 21:5–16). Elijah foretold that dogs would eat her at Jezreel (1 Kings 21:23), and she died thrown from a window at Jehu's order (2 Kings 9:30–37). A seal inscribed with her name is known, though whether it was hers is debated.
sections.refs: 1 Kings 16:31; 1 Kings 18:4; 1 Kings 18:19; 1 Kings 19:1–3; 1 Kings 21:5–25; 2 Kings 9:30–37

sections.b: Already in 2 Kings Jehu speaks of "your mother Jezebel" and "her prostitution and her many sorceries" (2 Kings 9:22), using the prophets' language for idolatry. By the time of Revelation her name stood for a teacher who led God's people into compromise with idols: "you leave the woman Jezebel alone, who calls herself a prophet" (Revelation 2:20). In later English "a Jezebel" became a slur for a shameless woman, a meaning the Bible itself does not give, and in the United States the name became a racist stereotype used against Black women from the time of slavery on. Jewish tradition could be kinder to her: a midrash says her skull, feet and hands were spared (2 Kings 9:35) because she used to clap and sing praise when a bride passed her palace and lament when mourners passed (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 17). Modern readers, including feminist scholars such as Phyllis Trible, ask how much of her portrait comes from her enemies, while noting that the text condemns Ahab with her (1 Kings 21:19–25).

common: Jezebel was a Phoenician princess from Tyre and Sidon who promoted Baal worship in Israel.
uncommon: Some scholars think the name Jezebel (Hebrew 'Izevel) was changed by Israelite writers from a Phoenician name meaning "Where is the prince?", a cry from the Baal myths, to a form that sounds like "dung."

sections.b: The Elijah stories are told as a contest with Baal on his own ground. The drought (1 Kings 17:1) strikes at the god said to bring dew and rain; the LORD feeds a widow with flour and oil in Phoenicia, Baal's homeland (1 Kings 17:8–16); and the LORD, not Baal, brings a dead boy back to life (1 Kings 17:22). On Carmel, Elijah lets Baal's prophets choose the test that should suit a storm god, fire from the sky, and mocks their god as perhaps lost in thought, away on a trip, or asleep (1 Kings 18:27), perhaps a jab at the myth of Baal's death and return. They limp around the altar and gash themselves as their custom was; "Not a sound" comes (1 Kings 18:26–29). The LORD answers with fire and then with rain. The struggle goes on: Ahaziah "served Baal and bowed down to him" (1 Kings 22:53).

common: Jezebel's Baal was probably a god of Tyre, either Baal Shamem or Melqart.
uncommon: Some scholars think Elijah's taunt "he has stepped away" (1 Kings 18:27) means Baal has gone to relieve himself.

sections.b: Elijah chose Carmel for the meeting of all Israel with the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:19–20). The ridge stood on the border with Phoenicia, caught the sea rains and may already have had altars to both gods; Elijah repairs an altar of the LORD that had been torn down (1 Kings 18:30). From its height his servant looks seven times toward the sea before the little cloud appears (1 Kings 18:42–44), and the Kishon River, where the prophets of Baal are killed, runs at its foot (1 Kings 18:40).

Naboth's vineyard lay beside Ahab's palace in Jezreel (1 Kings 21:1). Ahab offered a fair exchange or price; Naboth refused on the ground of the LORD's law (1 Kings 21:3). Jezebel used a public fast, two worthless men and a charge of cursing God and the king to have him stoned (1 Kings 21:8–14). Elijah's sentence, "Have you murdered, and taken possession as well?" (1 Kings 21:19), named the crime. The dogs that licked Ahab's blood (1 Kings 22:38), Ahab's delayed judgment (1 Kings 21:29) and the death of his son on Naboth's plot (2 Kings 9:25–26) all look back to this murder.

common: Naboth's vineyard is the Bible's best-known example of a ruler stealing land under cover of law.
uncommon: The Talmud identifies the lying spirit of 1 Kings 22:21 as the spirit of Naboth, seeking justice against Ahab.

sections.b: 1 Kings 20 and 22 tell of two Aramean attacks under Ben-hadad, defeated at Samaria and at Aphek, of Ahab's treaty with the defeated king, and of the war over Ramoth-gilead in which Ahab died (1 Kings 20:1–34; 1 Kings 22:1–36). The Arameans' theory that Israel's god ruled only the mountains is answered by a victory in the valley (1 Kings 20:23–28). At Horeb God tells Elijah to anoint Hazael king of Aram, the man who will punish Israel (1 Kings 19:15–17). Assyrian records complicate the picture: in 853 BC the king of Damascus, named Hadadezer, fought beside Ahab against Shalmaneser III.

sections.h: Prophets in the age of Elijah
sections.b: 1 Kings 17–22 shows prophets of many kinds. Elijah acts alone, at God's word, against the king. A hundred of the LORD's prophets hide in a cave, fed by the king's own steward (1 Kings 18:4). Bands of ecstatic prophets serve Baal (1 Kings 18:29). Unnamed prophets advise Ahab in war and promise victory (1 Kings 20:13–28). "Sons of the prophets" form a group with its own members (1 Kings 20:35). Four hundred court prophets speak "with one mouth" for the king, while one prophet, Micaiah, speaks against them (1 Kings 22:6–28). The test that settles who is right is the one in Deuteronomy: whether the word comes true (1 Kings 22:28; Deuteronomy 18:22).

The clearest Old Testament story of true and false prophets is 1 Kings 22. Four hundred prophets, fed by the king, promise victory in vague words ("the Lord will hand it over to the king") and act it out with iron horns (1 Kings 22:6, 22:11). One prophet, Micaiah, whom the king hates, says he will speak only what the LORD says, and tells of a lying spirit in the mouth of all the king's prophets (1 Kings 22:14–23). When struck and imprisoned, he appeals to the test of fulfillment (1 Kings 22:24–28). Jeremiah later meets the same problem in Hananiah and the prophets who say "peace" (Jeremiah 23:16–22; Jeremiah 28:8–9).

common: A true prophet may stand alone against a majority.
uncommon: The Talmud says Jehoshaphat suspected the four hundred because true prophets never speak in identical words.

sections.b: Micaiah's vision is set against the scene at Samaria's gate: two kings on thrones and four hundred prophets before them (1 Kings 22:10). Micaiah sees the true throne room, with the LORD seated and "all the army of heaven" on his right and left (1 Kings 22:19). The LORD asks a question, the members answer in different ways, and one spirit volunteers; the LORD approves and sends it (1 Kings 22:20–22). The council here has voices but no independent power: it carries out a sentence the LORD has already decided. Jeremiah's claim that the false prophets had not "stood in the council of the LORD" (Jeremiah 23:18) may look back to this scene.

In Micaiah's vision a spirit offers to "be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets," and the LORD sends it (1 Kings 22:21–23). Interpreters have identified it as an angel of the council, the spirit of prophecy acting as a false message, Satan, or (in the Talmud) the spirit of Naboth (Bavli Sanhedrin 89a). Its work raises the question whether God deceives. Main answers: God permits deception as judgment on one who has refused the truth (Ezekiel 14:9; 2 Thessalonians 2:11); the vision itself warns Ahab plainly, so he is not deceived without being told (R. W. L. Moberly); the scene is a prophetic parable; or it reflects an early way of tracing all things to God, later refined (compare 1 Chronicles 21:1).

common: God is not said to lie in 1 Kings 22; a spirit does, and Micaiah reveals it.
uncommon: Some readers take Micaiah's vision as a parable, not a report of a real heavenly debate.

sections.b: The first person God sends Elijah to is a foreign widow gathering sticks for her last meal (1 Kings 17:9–12). She shares her handful of flour and finds that the jar and the jug do not run out (1 Kings 17:13–16). When her son dies she blames the prophet, and Elijah's prayer brings him back (1 Kings 17:17–24). Jesus told his hometown that of all the widows in Israel, Elijah was sent to this one in Sidon (Luke 4:25–26), and Luke's widow of Nain recalls her story (Luke 7:11–17).

The widow of Zarephath gives a stranger from a hostile nation water, bread and, later, her upstairs room (1 Kings 17:10–19). Her hospitality is costly: the bread is the last she has. The story belongs with Abraham's welcome to the three visitors (Genesis 18:1–8) and the Shunammite's room for Elisha (2 Kings 4:8–10), where the host is rewarded with a son's life. Hebrews' saying that some have welcomed angels without knowing it is often read alongside these stories (Hebrews 13:2).

Elijah is the only person after Moses whom the Bible brings back to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8). He walks there forty days and forty nights, as Moses stayed forty days on the mountain (Exodus 24:18; Exodus 34:28), spends the night in "the cave," and hears that the LORD will "pass by," the word of Exodus 33:19–22. Wind, quake and fire, the signs of Sinai, come, but the LORD is not in them; then comes "a sound of thin silence" (1 Kings 19:11–12). Elijah wraps his face, as Moses covered his at the bush (Exodus 3:6), and receives a new commission.

1 Kings 19 deliberately tells Elijah's flight as a return to Moses: forty days and nights without other food, the mountain of God, a cave like the cleft of the rock, God passing by, a covered face, and a successor who begins as his servant, as Joshua did (1 Kings 19:8–21; Exodus 24:13; Exodus 33:22). The parallels continue in 2 Kings: Elijah parts the Jordan as Moses parted the sea, and is taken away east of the Jordan where Moses died (2 Kings 2:8–11; Deuteronomy 34:1–6). So the two appear together at the end of the prophets (Malachi 4:4–5) and on the mountain of the Transfiguration (Mark 9:4).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 19:8–21; Exodus 24:13; Exodus 33:22; 2 Kings 2:8–11; Malachi 4:4–5; Mark 9:4

sections.h: Not in the wind, the quake or the fire
sections.b: At Horeb the LORD passes by Elijah, but the text says three times what God was not in: the wind, the earthquake and the fire (1 Kings 19:11–12). Then comes qol demamah daqqah, "a sound of thin silence." Elijah does not see God; he hears, covers his face and goes out (1 Kings 19:13). The scene became a classic text for the idea that God is known more in stillness than in spectacle, though readers differ on whether the silence corrects the fire of Carmel or simply shows God's freedom.

Carmel is the Old Testament's great public test of the claim that only the LORD is God. Elijah's question, how long Israel will limp along on two crutches (1 Kings 18:21), assumes Israel was trying to worship both. The test is framed in terms of who is "the God" (ha-Elohim), and the people's answer repeats it (1 Kings 18:24, 18:39). In chapter 20 the Arameans think the LORD is a god of the mountains only, and he proves himself God of the valleys too (1 Kings 20:23–28).

sections.h: The ban and the slaughter in Elijah's time
sections.b: Two scenes in 1 Kings 17–22 raise the hardest questions of holy war. Elijah has the prophets of Baal killed at the Kishon (1 Kings 18:40), acting on the law against prophets who lead Israel to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). And a prophet condemns Ahab for releasing Ben-hadad, "the man I put under the ban" (1 Kings 20:42), as Saul was condemned for sparing Agag (1 Samuel 15). Readers divide over whether to read these as just covenant judgments for their time, as stories later writers told in a struggle against Baal worship, or as acts the rest of Scripture corrects (Luke 9:54–55).

Naboth's refusal shows how seriously Israel took the land as the LORD's gift: "The LORD keep me from giving you my fathers' inheritance!" (1 Kings 21:3; see Leviticus 25:23; Numbers 36:7). The chapter uses the conquest verb "take possession" four times of Ahab's seizure of the vineyard (1 Kings 21:15–19), and compares Ahab to the Amorites whom the LORD drove out (1 Kings 21:26), hinting that Israel's kings could lose the land the same way.

Jezebel's plot against Naboth keeps every form of justice and breaks its spirit: a public fast, a trial before the elders, the two witnesses the Law required, a charge of cursing God and the king, and stoning outside the town (1 Kings 21:9–13; Deuteronomy 17:6; Exodus 22:28). The Law's answer to false witness was to do to the witness what he meant to do to the accused (Deuteronomy 19:16–19); here it is God who brings the sentence on the king's house (1 Kings 21:19–24). Christian readers have seen the same pattern in the trials of Jesus and of Stephen (Mark 14:55–59; Acts 6:11–13).

The most surprising repentance in Kings is Ahab's. After Elijah's sentence he tears his clothes, wears sackcloth, fasts and walks about quietly, and the LORD tells Elijah, "Do you see that Ahab has humbled himself before me?" (1 Kings 21:27–29). The judgment is not cancelled but delayed to his son's days. Readers use the passage both to show the reach of God's mercy and to ask how repentance and judgment fit together, a question Jonah and Ezekiel also raise (Jonah 3:10; Ezekiel 18:21–23).

Naboth's story sets two ideas of kingship side by side. Ahab offers to buy the vineyard and accepts the refusal, sulking but not seizing. Jezebel asks whether that is any way to rule as king over Israel (1 Kings 21:7) and takes what the king wants. Israel's law limited its kings (Deuteronomy 17:14–20; 1 Samuel 8:11–18), and the prophet calls the king to account in the king's own vineyard (1 Kings 21:17–24). In chapter 22 Micaiah's image of the king as a shepherd whose sheep are scattered shows what was at stake (1 Kings 22:17).

At Horeb God tells Elijah to anoint Hazael king of Aram, Jehu king of Israel and Elisha as prophet in his place (1 Kings 19:15–16). This is the only command in the Bible to anoint a prophet, and Elijah carries it out with his cloak rather than oil (1 Kings 19:19). The other two anointings happen through Elisha in 2 Kings: Hazael is told he will be king (2 Kings 8:13), and a son of the prophets pours oil on Jehu (2 Kings 9:1–6).

sections.h: Elijah's power to shut the sky
sections.b: Revelation's witnesses "have authority to shut the sky" (Revelation 11:6) as Elijah did when he swore that no dew or rain would fall except at his word (1 Kings 17:1), and fire comes from their mouths as fire came down at Elijah's word (1 Kings 18:38; 2 Kings 1:10). The 1,260 days of their prophesying match the three and a half years of Elijah's drought in Luke 4:25 and James 5:17.
sections.refs: 1 Kings 17:1; 1 Kings 18:1; 1 Kings 18:38; Revelation 11:3–6; Luke 4:25; James 5:17

sections.b: The New Testament reads Elijah as a pattern. John the Baptist comes with "Elijah's spirit and power" (Luke 1:17), dressed like him in hair and leather (2 Kings 1:8; Mark 1:6), and like Elijah he confronts a king and a queen (Mark 6:17–18). Jesus' raising of the widow's son at Nain echoes Elijah's at Zarephath (1 Kings 17:23; Luke 7:15), and his forty days in the wilderness echo Elijah's journey to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8; Matthew 4:2).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 17:17–24; 1 Kings 19:8; Luke 1:17; Luke 7:11–17; Mark 1:6; Mark 6:17–18; Matthew 4:2

sections.b: Elijah prays for the widow's son and the LORD hears him (1 Kings 17:20–22). On Carmel his short prayer, "Answer me, LORD! Answer me!" (1 Kings 18:37), contrasts with the long cries of Baal's prophets. On the mountaintop he crouches with his face between his knees until the rain comes (1 Kings 18:42–45). James takes these scenes as the model of a righteous person's prayer: Elijah was a man like us, he prayed, and the sky gave rain (James 5:16–18).

The Deuteronomistic writers liked to show a prophet's word and its later fulfillment. Elijah's sentence on Ahab (1 Kings 21:19–24) is fulfilled step by step: the dogs lick Ahab's blood "according to the word the LORD had spoken" (1 Kings 22:38), and Jezebel and Joram die at Jezreel (2 Kings 9:25–37). Critical scholars note seams in the pattern, such as the place of the dogs and the delay announced in 1 Kings 21:29, and see an editor joining older stories into one scheme.

sections.h: The Greek order of 1 Kings 20–21 and the kaige section
sections.b: In the Greek translation (3 Kingdoms), the Naboth story comes before the wars with Aram, so that chapters 20 and 22 stand together and the Elijah stories form one block. Scholars disagree about which order is older. From 1 Kings 22 to the end of 2 Kings, Codex Vaticanus, and so the standard Rahlfs edition, carries the kaige revision, which brought the Greek closer to the Hebrew; the Lucianic (Antiochene) manuscripts there are the better witness to the Old Greek (H. St. J. Thackeray; D. Barthélemy).

When Elijah announces judgment for Naboth's murder, Ahab tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, fasts and goes about quietly (1 Kings 21:27). God tells Elijah that Ahab "has humbled himself before me" and delays the disaster until his son's reign (21:29). Even this king's fast is treated as real humbling.

Elijah thinks he alone is left, but God keeps seven thousand in Israel who have not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:18). Paul reads the verse as a picture of election: a remnant "chosen by grace" (Romans 11:4–5).
